ATP effect hypotheses — which pathways, and how good is the resulting fit

The question. Low ATP makes cardiac muscle stronger and slower. In this model every ATP effect is a multiplicative gate on a rate, and 21 rates are gateable. Which of them should be allowed to feel [ATP]?

That is a model-selection question, not a fitting question, so it is answered first — §1–§3 — and only then is the resulting fit shown against the data (§4–§6).

Answer, on the current core (spreadw_iter_018): two gates. k2 (ATP-induced actomyosin detachment) and kah (hydrolysis / re-priming) capture 99.5 % of the entire ATP effect. Every remaining gate — including all four SRX gates and kamh, the third CHEM gate — stays at exactly zero or buys only mechanics.

1. The ladder

Core model frozen at spreadw_iter_018; only ATP-gate exponents refitted. Every gate is exactly 1 at MgATP_ref, so the 8 mM fit is invariant by construction — asserted at |Δ| = 0.000e+00 before any fitting. The 2 mM objective (19 features) includes force-velocity. Accept threshold 0.32 = 3× the measured noise peak-to-peak.

rung gates which DOF 2 mM cost % of span
H0 none no ATP effect at all 0 385.13 0 %
H1 CHEM k2, kah, kamh 3 8.2013 99.51 %
H2 + SRX kmsrd, ksr0, ksr2srd, ksrd2sr 7 8.2013 99.51 %
H3 + MECH eta_M, kSE, mu_neg 10 7.6429 99.66 %
H4 all 21 + the rest 21 6.4333 100 %

Fitted exponents — only five gates of 21 are ever non-zero:

gate class H1 H2 H3 H4
k2 CHEM 0.440 0.440 0.440 0.440
kah CHEM 0.300 0.300 0.300 0.300
kamh CHEM 0 0 0 0
all four SRX SRX — 0 0 0
eta_M MECH — — −0.150 −0.150
kSE MECH — — 0 +0.070
kSE_M OTHER — — — −0.150

Three results, in order of importance:

  1. Two gates do essentially everything. k2 and kah take the fit from 385.13 to 8.20 — 99.5 % of the whole span. Both are unambiguous ATP chemistry: the nucleotide is a substrate of the step. kamh never moves off zero.
  2. The SRX gates buy exactly nothing. H2 completed a full sweep of all seven gates and accepted none; H2 = H1 to four decimals.
  3. Everything beyond that is mechanics. H3's gain is eta_M alone (−0.56); H4 adds kSE and kSE_M for a further −1.21. All three are viscosity or spring terms with no nucleotide chemistry. The "any rate can feel ATP" hypothesis does not discover an ATP pathway — it bends compliance, exactly as it did on the previous core.
This supersedes an earlier version of this report, which was built on joint82_opt and concluded that seven gates were needed and that the SRX gates earned their place via k_tr. On a core where rsK and force-velocity are properly fitted, they do not: they were compensating for that core's defects. §8 has the details and the correction history.

The classification is by chemistry, decided before fitting:

  • CHEM — the nucleotide is a substrate of the step. k2 is ATP-induced actomyosin dissociation (without it there is no cycle); kah/kamh are hydrolysis and its reverse.
  • SRX — no ATP in the rate law as written, but the states differ in bound nucleotide, so an ATP dependence is arguable.
  • MECH / OTHER — stiffness, viscosity, geometry, actin attachment, the power stroke. An ATP dependence here is phenomenology, not mechanism.

H4 never converged — 21 gates × 4 steps needs ~84 evaluations per sweep and its budget allowed one. 13.79 is a floor, not an optimum, and the comparison is deliberately generous to it. It still loses on every per-DOF measure, and its whole advantage comes from kSE_M (a Maxwell spring, −0.52) and tau_reg (a geometric recovery time, −0.32).

Cost differences of 0.3 are hard to interpret. These are the same three hypotheses drawn against the 3-preparation 2 mM envelope, so the question becomes "does the extra freedom fix a feature that was outside the data's own spread?"

3. Why H2, specifically

The SRX gates earn their place on exactly one feature: k_tr. H1 → H2 moves it from +1.7 SD to −0.1 SD — from outside the between-preparation envelope to essentially exact. Look at the k_tr panel: the orange (H1) curve sits above the data at every cycle; red and purple lie on it. Everything else moves by ≤ 0.3 SD.

That is a real, localised, physiologically coherent gain — SRX-return kinetics setting isometric force redevelopment — and it is worth four parameters.

The mechanical gates do not earn theirs. H2 → H3 improves the mean |SD| by 0.10. The only feature that moves is rsK (10.7 → 8.8), still catastrophically outside the envelope either way; peak1_dSL gets worse (2.4 → 2.9). No feature crosses into the envelope. Three parameters, no defect fixed.

So the cost ladder and the feature-space picture agree, and they agree on H2.

Everything below therefore uses params/lowATP_H2_chem_opt.m — the H2 rung — and one parameter file gives both conditions: the 8 mM and 2 mM curves differ only by [MgATP], not by a second fit.

4. The ATP effect, model vs data

Ratios are formed per preparation and then averaged, so the SD is the real between-prep spread of the effect, not of the levels.

feature data 2/8 ±SD model inside ±1 SD?
steady 1.376 0.246 1.160 yes
A 0.993 0.057 1.025 yes
peak1_y 1.039 0.177 1.059 yes
vall_y 1.027 0.102 0.927 yes
peak2 1.011 0.107 0.909 yes
vall2_dy 0.970 0.178 1.464 no
ktr 0.540 0.051 0.506 yes
rsK 0.345 0.061 0.627 no
restretchSlopeStart 1.265 0.310 1.085 yes
peak1_dSL 1.293 0.568 1.219 yes
vall_t 0.950 0.552 1.113 yes
rsR2 1.187 0.101 1.001 no — artifact, see below

The model reproduces the ATP effect within between-preparation scatter for 10 of 12 features. Only vall2_dy and rsK genuinely fail.

Structural point worth more than the cost numbers: once each preparation is scaled by its own steady force, most features show no ATP effect at all — A, peak1_y, vall_y, peak2, vall2_dy all sit at 1.0 ± 0.1 in the data. The 2 mM phenotype is a force scale-up plus two rate slowdowns, not a change of waveform shape, and the model gets that structure right.

rsR2 is a non-defect: the model is a noise-free single exponential, so its restretch-recovery R² pins at 1.000 against the data's 0.87. Bounded 0.4–1.0 in the objective; scores zero either way.

Absolute force: 2 mM 84.7 ± 6.1 kPa vs 8 mM 63.3 ± 14.8 kPa = ×1.34, independently consistent with ATPEffectReconciliation's rundown-corrected ×1.36. The 8 mM spread is 3× wider (CV 23 % vs 7 %), which is why steady carries the loosest error bar despite being the largest effect.

5. Force-velocity, both conditions

The model separates the conditions in the right direction and by about the right amount. Two residuals:

  • 8 mM mid-velocity concavity — +6 % at 0.5 ML/s, −20 % at 2 ML/s, pinned correctly at both ends. A curvature error, so the lever is the strain dependence of detachment, not a scalar rate.
  • 2 mM power peak position. Data peak power is at v = 1.0 ML/s at both concentrations; the model puts the 2 mM peak at 0.5. An earlier report of mine offered that leftward shift as a falsifiable prediction and claimed the data did not exist. It did — Data_ATP column 4 — and it falsifies the prediction.

6. The low-ATP fit against the 3-preparation envelope

Every trace and force-dimension feature is divided by its own mean steady before averaging, because absolute force is not transferable between preparations. The band is the spread of the shape. 03/27 — the fit target — is drawn separately: a deviation from the mean is only a defect if it is also a deviation from 03/27.

Model steady 88.8 kPa against 84.7 ± 6.1 — inside 1 SD. The model tracks 03/27 almost exactly through cycles 1–3. The systematic error is confined to the re-stretch spike (model 1.35 vs data 1.18 at cycle 1, in every cycle) and to cycles 4–5, where 03/27 is itself at the top of the band.

There is no 2 mM staircase dataset — only 8 mM tables exist. That panel is the 2 mM model as an unconstrained prediction against the 8 mM trace; the 0.035 cost is against 8 mM data. Shown for completeness, not as evidence.

7. Where the residual actually is

Stripping the non-defect (rsR2) and everything inside between-preparation scatter, three problems remain — and two are the same problem:

  1. rsK — post-restretch recovery, ×1.8 too fast as a ratio, +10.7 SD absolute.
  2. The re-stretch spike overshoots in every cycle: vall2_dy (−3.9 SD) and peak1_dSL (+2.4 SD). Same window as (1).
  3. vall_t (+6.1 SD) — model 12–18 ms vs data 3–8 ms. A sub-10 ms timing error, low-weighted, but real.

Everything in the low-ATP phenotype outside the re-stretch window is reproduced within the spread of the data. And rsK is not an ATP-pathway question: no rung of the ladder moves it below +8.8 SD, and it is 60 % off at 8 mM too.

8. Core history, and what changed when it was corrected

§1 is fitted on spreadw_iter_018. §4–§7 are still on the previous core (joint82_opt) and are being regenerated; treat their absolute numbers as stale until this note is removed. The selection conclusion in §1–§3 is the current one.

Which core, and why it matters. Scored on one objective (realign4's feature list, 8 mM full battery):

snapshot 8 mM Et FV power rsK term rsK s⁻¹ (data 43.7)
spreadw_iter_018 4.4084 0.0898 0.0504 50.1 (×1.15)
realign4_opt 3.8519 1.3427 0.3810 66.0 (×1.51)
joint82_opt 4.0101 1.3853 0.4582 69.3 (×1.59)

spreadw_iter_018 is identical to spreadw_opt — it is the final optimum, not an intermediate. Its total is worse because it was fitted on the reweighted (λ/s² between-prep spread) objective, but the two components that carry information are transformed: force-velocity power 15× better, rsK 7.6× better.

Two corrections this forced, both of which changed conclusions:

  1. rsK was never the open defect it appeared to be. It was solved in RestretchSRXRecoil (load realignment, ×2.35 → ×1.12). joint82_opt traded that fix away, and three analyses — including earlier versions of this one — were seeded from the traded-away core, which is why rsK kept re-appearing as the headline problem. On the current core it is ×1.15 of data.
  2. The SRX gates do not earn their place. On joint82_opt, H1→H2 was the decisive step and moved k_tr from +1.7 SD to −0.1 SD. On spreadw_iter_018 the SRX gates accept nothing at all. That gain was compensation for the core, not physiology.

Process fixes, so this class of error is harder to repeat: the core snapshot is now an explicit top-of-file CORE option in RunAtpHypothesisOptim.m rather than buried in a loadParams call, and AuditBaselines8mM.m scores candidate cores like-for-like.

Two bugs in the optimiser were caught by its own dry run and are worth recording: clear at the top of a script wiped caller-set options (silently turning DRYRUN=true into a live 8-hour fit), and a budget-truncated rung was labelled CONVERGED, which led to a published claim that the mechanical gates buy nothing when that rung had never tested them. Both fixed; conv now requires a completed full sweep.

Drivers: RunHypothesisComparison.m (§2–3), RunAtpHeadToHead.m (§4–5), RunLowAtpFitReport.m (§6). All standalone; the last two can run in parallel.
